newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's Sacob says growth below 2.5 pct possible.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's Sacob says growth below 2.5 pct possible.

text.p: The South African economy still appeared set for a soft landing this year but there were signs that GDP growth could come in even below the forecast 2.5 percent, the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) said.
"There are a number of factors which could tip the balance and result in even weaker growth (than the forecast 2.5 percent)," director of economic policy Ben van Rensburg told reporters on Wednesday.

Sacob earlier reported a 0.3 percentage point rise in its business confidence index to 114.0 in April but it cautioned that the business mood was under threat by perceptions that crime was not being dealt with effectively.

"Crime remains the greatest single threat to continued business confidence," van Rensburg said, referring to the slaying last week of top South African economist Ronnie Bethlehem and the continued assault on banks.
Among factors militating against a stronger growth rate were the recovery of the rand since the beginning of the year, high interest rates and the balance of payments influence.
Expectations of strong export-led growth were being dampened by the relatively strong currency, van Rensburg said.

In addition, contradictory forces such as reduced government expenditure and contradictory monetary policy -- as the Reserve Bank managed the liberalisation of exchange controls and the withdrawal from the forward market -- would keep a lid on the growth rate.
Government's macro-economic strategy plan released in June last year envisages a growth rate of 2.9 percent in 1997.
It was increasingly unlikely that interest rates would fall before the third quarter if even then, Sacob said.

"While we acknowledge that interest rates are one of the mechanisms to help smooth exchange control liberalisation, the current state of the economy suggests the central bank needs to ...reduce interest rates as soon as possible," it said.
Positive influences on the business mood in April were the inflow of short-term foreign capital, the stability of the rand and the possible peak in the inflation rate.
On the negative side, crime had rocketed and the ability of the economy to meet the need for job creation remained poor.
In the manufacturing sector, expectations for sales and production volumes to increase during the year were more subdued than the first few months of the year.
